questions.stem: Choose the sentence that has the CORRECT question tag for the clause 'She hardly speaks in meetings'.

options.option_text: She hardly speaks in meetings, doesn't she?
She hardly speaks in meetings, does she?
She hardly speaks in meetings, isn't she?
She hardly speaks in meetings, hasn't she?

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Hardly' is a semi-negative adverb (like rarely, seldom, barely, scarcely). When the main clause contains such a word, it carries an implicit negative meaning, so the question tag must be POSITIVE ('does she?'). Option A ('doesn't she') is the classic trap — students treat 'hardly' as a neutral adverb and apply the standard affirmative-clause rule. Rule: Negative adverbs (hardly, rarely, seldom, barely) → positive question tag. Example applying the same rule: 'He barely eats anything, does he?' — the positive tag 'does he' is mandatory here too.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a correctly formed FIRST conditional sentence?

options.option_text: If it will rain, we shall cancel the match and go home early
If it rains, we shall cancel the match and go home early
If it rained, we shall cancel the match and go home early
If it rains, we would cancel the match and go home early

questions.explanation: B is correct. First conditional (real/possible future) rule: if-clause = Simple Present tense; main clause = will/shall + base verb. Option A is the most common error — 'will' must NEVER appear in the if-clause of a first conditional ('If it will rain' is wrong). Option C uses 'rained' (simple past), which belongs to the second conditional. Option D uses 'would', which signals a second conditional (unreal present). Rule summary: If + V1 (present), will/shall + V1. Example: 'If you study hard, you will pass.' — same structure.

questions.stem: Which sentence is grammatically CORRECT in the SECOND conditional?

options.option_text: If I was rich, I would travel across all seven continents of the world
If I were rich, I would travel across all seven continents of the world
If I were rich, I will travel across all seven continents of the world
If I am rich, I would travel across all seven continents of the world

questions.explanation: B is correct. Second conditional (unreal present/hypothetical) rule: if-clause uses PAST SUBJUNCTIVE 'were' for ALL persons (including 'I'), and the main clause uses would/could/might + base verb. Option A ('was') is colloquially used but is marked incorrect in SSC/bank exams, which test formal grammar where 'were' is mandatory for the subjunctive mood. Option C uses 'will' (future, real) instead of 'would' (hypothetical), making it a first conditional error. Option D uses simple present 'am', treating the condition as factual rather than unreal. Example: 'If he were the director, he would revamp the policy.' — 'were' is required even for third person singular.

questions.stem: If the medicine ___ on time, the patient would not have deteriorated so rapidly.

options.option_text: had arrived — past perfect correctly used in third conditional
arrived — simple past tense used without perfective aspect
would have arrived — modal perfect incorrectly placed in if-clause
has arrived — present perfect incorrectly used in if-clause

questions.explanation: A is correct. Third conditional (unreal past) rule: if-clause = Past Perfect (had + V3); main clause = would/could/might + have + V3. 'Had arrived' is the correct past perfect form. Option C ('would have arrived') is the most tempting error — 'would have' belongs only in the MAIN clause, never in the if-clause of any conditional. Option B ('arrived') is simple past, which belongs in second conditional if-clauses expressing unreal present. Option D ('has arrived') is present perfect, which has no role in conditional structures. Example applying the rule: 'If they had left earlier, they would have caught the flight.' — same pattern.

questions.stem: Select the sentence in which 'unless' is used INCORRECTLY.

options.option_text: Unless you apologise, she will not forgive you for the mistake
Unless he doesn't study harder, he will fail the final examination
Unless it rains, the festival will be held outdoors as planned
Unless you confirm your attendance, your seat will be cancelled

questions.explanation: B is incorrect. 'Unless' already carries the meaning 'if...not', so pairing it with a negative verb ('doesn't') creates a double negative: 'Unless he doesn't study harder' = 'If he does not not study harder' — which reverses the intended meaning entirely. The correct form is: 'Unless he studies harder, he will fail.' Rule: Unless + affirmative verb = if + negative verb. Options A, C, and D are all correct — each uses an affirmative verb after 'unless', preserving the negative conditional logic. Example: 'Unless you hurry (= if you do not hurry), you will miss the train.' — note the affirmative 'hurry' after 'unless'.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences is a MIXED conditional expressing an unreal past cause with a present consequence?

options.option_text: If she had joined the army, she would be a colonel by now
If she had joined the army, she would have been a colonel now
If she joined the army, she would be a colonel by now
If she joins the army, she will be a colonel in the future

questions.explanation: A is correct. A mixed conditional combines: Past Perfect in the if-clause (unreal PAST cause: 'had joined') + 'would + base verb' in the main clause (PRESENT consequence: 'would be a colonel by now'). Option B is pure third conditional — 'would have been' signals a PAST result, not a present one; the time-marker 'now' does not change its grammatical class. Option C is pure second conditional ('if she joined' = unreal present, not unreal past). Option D is a first conditional (real future). The diagnostic signal: if-clause has Past Perfect AND main clause has 'would + base verb' (not 'would have'), the sentence is a mixed conditional. Example: 'If he had exercised regularly, he would be fit today.' — same structure.

questions.stem: Identify the grammatically CORRECT inverted conditional (where 'if' has been dropped and the auxiliary fronted).

options.option_text: Were she to invest wisely, she would double her returns within a year
Was she to invest wisely, she would double her returns within a year
Were she to invest wisely, she will double her returns within a year
Should she to invest wisely, she would double her returns within a year

questions.explanation: A is correct. Inverted conditionals omit 'if' and front the auxiliary. For a second conditional subjunctive ('If she were to invest'), the inversion uses 'Were + subject + to + base verb': 'Were she to invest wisely, she would...' — 'were' is mandatory regardless of person or number. Option B ('Was she to') fails because 'was' can NEVER replace 'were' in subjunctive inversion; the subjunctive form 'were' is the only acceptable auxiliary here. Option C ('she will') switches the main clause to future tense, converting a second conditional (hypothetical) into a first conditional (real future) — structurally inconsistent. Option D ('Should she to') is doubly wrong: 'should' is used to invert first conditionals ('Should it rain, we will cancel'), and 'should' inversion NEVER takes 'to' after it ('Should she invest', not 'Should she to invest'). Example: 'Were I the CEO, I would overhaul the process.' — same inversion pattern.
